text: Can you give me some phrases for ordering at a restaurant?

Of course. These cover a whole meal, from sitting down to paying:

Getting a table
- ¿Tienen una mesa libre? (Do you have a free table?)
- Una mesa para dos, por favor. (A table for two, please.)

Ordering
- ¿Me trae la carta, por favor? (Could you bring me the menu, please?)
- ¿Qué me recomienda? (What do you recommend?)
- ¿Qué lleva este plato? (What's in this dish?)
- Quisiera el pollo, por favor. (I'd like the chicken, please.)
- Para mí, la sopa. (For me, the soup.)
- Para beber, un agua con gas. (To drink, a sparkling water.)
- Sin hielo, por favor. (Without ice, please.)

During the meal
- ¿Me puede traer más pan? (Can you bring me more bread?)
- Está delicioso. (It's delicious.)
- Perdone, ¿me puede traer una servilleta? (Excuse me, could you bring me a napkin?)

Paying
- La cuenta, por favor. (The check, please.)
- ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta? (Can I pay by card?)
- ¿Está incluida la propina? (Is the tip included?)

A couple of grammar notes:
- Quisiera is a polite form of 'I want.' It's softer than quiero and always safe in a restaurant.
- Me trae and me puede traer use the formal usted form, which is the normal way to speak to a server in most places.
- Para mí is a very handy shortcut. You can say para mí plus almost any dish name and be understood.

Here's a set that covers asking and, just as important, understanding the answer.

Asking
- Perdone, ¿dónde está la estación de tren? (Excuse me, where is the train station?)
- ¿Cómo llego al museo? (How do I get to the museum?)
- ¿Está lejos? (Is it far?)
- ¿Está cerca de aquí? (Is it near here?)
- ¿Hay una farmacia por aquí? (Is there a pharmacy around here?)
- ¿Se puede ir a pie? (Can you walk there?)

Understanding the answer
- Siga todo recto. (Go straight ahead.)
- Gire a la derecha. (Turn right.)
- Gire a la izquierda. (Turn left.)
- En la esquina. (On the corner.)
- A dos cuadras. (Two blocks away. In Spain you'll hear manzanas instead of cuadras.)
- Al lado de... (Next to...)
- Enfrente de... (Across from...)
- Detrás de... (Behind...)

When you miss part of it
- Más despacio, por favor. (Slower, please.)
- ¿Me lo puede mostrar en el mapa? (Can you show me on the map?)
- Muchas gracias, muy amable. (Thank you very much, that's very kind.)

A tip: derecha (right) and derecho (straight, in many Latin American countries) sound alike and are easy to mix up. If someone says siga derecho, they mean keep going straight, not turn right.
Could you help with numbers too?

Sure. Numbers come up constantly, especially with prices and times, so they're worth drilling.

1 to 10
uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez

The tens
veinte (20), treinta (30), cuarenta (40), cincuenta (50), sesenta (60), setenta (70), ochenta (80), noventa (90), cien (100)

Building numbers
- From 21 to 29, they're written as one word: veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés, and so on.
- From 31 up, you join with y: treinta y uno (31), cuarenta y cinco (45), noventa y nueve (99).
- 100 is cien on its own, but ciento when followed by more: ciento veinte (120).

Useful phrases
- ¿Cuánto cuesta? (How much does it cost?)
- ¿Cuánto es? (How much is it? Used when paying.)
- Son veinte pesos. (It's twenty pesos.)
- ¿Qué hora es? (What time is it?)
- Son las tres y media. (It's three thirty.)
- Es la una. (It's one o'clock. Note la una is singular.)

Practice idea
Whenever you see a price tag or a clock, say the number in Spanish in your head. It sounds simple, but it builds speed quickly, and speed is what matters when someone tells you a price out loud.

Here are some that keep a friendly conversation going:

Greetings
- Mucho gusto. / Encantada. (Nice to meet you. A woman says encantada, a man encantado.)
- ¿Qué tal? (How's it going?)
- Muy bien, ¿y tú? (Very well, and you?)
- Más o menos. (So-so.)

The weather
- Hace buen tiempo hoy. (The weather's nice today.)
- Hace mucho calor. (It's very hot.)
- Hace frío. (It's cold.)
- Está lloviendo. (It's raining.)

Showing interest
- ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?)
- ¿Qué tal el fin de semana? (How was the weekend?)
- ¡Qué interesante! (How interesting!)
- ¿En serio? (Really?)
- ¡Qué bien! (That's great!)

Keeping it going
- ¿Y tú? (And you?)
- Perdona, no entendí. (Sorry, I didn't understand.)
- ¿Cómo se dice ... en español? (How do you say ... in Spanish?)

Saying goodbye
- Hasta luego. (See you later.)
- Nos vemos. (See you.)
- Que te vaya bien. (Take care.)

A note on tú and usted: these use tú, which is fine with classmates and people your age in casual settings. With someone older or in a formal setting, switch to usted: ¿Y usted? instead of ¿Y tú?
How should I practice these between lessons?

Short, frequent practice beats one long session. Here's a routine that fits in 10 to 15 minutes a day:

1. Flashcards with spaced repetition (5 minutes)
Put the phrases into Anki or a similar app with English on one side and Spanish on the other. Spaced repetition shows you each card right before you'd forget it, which is very efficient. Practice in both directions, but English to Spanish is the harder and more useful one.

2. Say everything out loud (3 minutes)
Read each phrase out loud rather than in your head. Speaking is a physical skill, and your mouth needs the practice as much as your memory does.

3. Shadowing (3 minutes)
Find a short audio clip of a native speaker, play a sentence, pause, and repeat it right away, copying the rhythm and intonation. Language-learning podcasts like Coffee Break Spanish work well for this.

4. Narrate small moments (anytime)
When you do something ordinary, say a simple phrase about it: Hace frío hoy, Son las siete, ¿Dónde están las llaves? It turns idle moments into practice.

5. Review the week before class (10 minutes)
The day before your lesson, go back over the week's phrases so they're fresh, and write down one or two questions to ask your teacher.

And don't worry about mistakes. Saying something imperfectly out loud teaches you more than saying it perfectly in your head.
Can you write a short practice dialogue at a café using some of these?

Here's one. Try reading both parts out loud, then cover the Spanish and try to produce it from the English.

Camarero: Buenas tardes. ¿Qué le pongo?
(Good afternoon. What can I get you?)

Cliente: Buenas tardes. Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.
(Good afternoon. I'd like a coffee with milk, please.)

Camarero: ¿Algo más?
(Anything else?)

Cliente: Sí, ¿qué me recomienda para comer?
(Yes, what do you recommend to eat?)

Camarero: La tortilla está muy rica hoy.
(The tortilla is very good today.)

Cliente: Perfecto, para mí la tortilla.
(Perfect, the tortilla for me.)

Camarero: Muy bien. ¿Para tomar aquí o para llevar?
(Very good. For here or to go?)

Cliente: Para tomar aquí. ¿Cuánto es?
(For here. How much is it?)

Camarero: Son seis euros.
(That's six euros.)

Cliente: ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta?
(Can I pay by card?)

Camarero: Sí, claro.
(Yes, of course.)

Cliente: Muchas gracias, muy amable.
(Thank you very much, that's very kind.)

Notes
- ¿Qué le pongo? is a very common way for staff to ask for your order in Spain. In Latin America you'll more often hear ¿Qué le sirvo? or ¿Qué va a tomar?
- In Spain, a tortilla is a potato omelet; in Mexico and Central America, it's the flatbread.
- Para llevar (to go) is worth memorizing on its own.
Could you quiz me on a few?

Sure. Try to say each one out loud in Spanish before looking at the answers below.

1. Could you bring me the menu, please?
2. Where is the train station?
3. Turn left.
4. How much does it cost?
5. It's three thirty.
6. The weather's nice today.
7. Sorry, I didn't understand.
8. For here or to go?
9. Slower, please.
10. See you later.

Answers
1. ¿Me trae la carta, por favor?
2. ¿Dónde está la estación de tren?
3. Gire a la izquierda.
4. ¿Cuánto cuesta?
5. Son las tres y media.
6. Hace buen tiempo hoy.
7. Perdona, no entendí.
8. ¿Para tomar aquí o para llevar?
9. Más despacio, por favor.
10. Hasta luego.

If you got seven or more, you're in good shape. Put any you missed at the top of your flashcard deck for the next few days, and they'll stick quickly.
